title: atlas-etl — turning raw downloads into the atlas's graph

overview.l1: This is the factory floor. Every raw file the project downloaded — the King James Bible as JSON, a spreadsheet of cross-references, a database of Bible places and people, Luther's Small Catechism, the entire Book of Concord, a 1921 Bible commentary, a file marking which words Jesus spoke — gets read here, cleaned up, checked for mistakes, and turned into tidy files under data/compiled/. If this crate vanished, the app would have raw text files nobody could use, and no way to catch a typo in the project's own hand-typed notes before it reached a reader. Nothing here talks to the internet — it only reads files already saved to disk and writes new ones.
overview.l2: atlas-etl is a library crate (`src/lib.rs` declares its modules) plus one binary (`src/main.rs`) and a small second binary (`src/bins/gen_sources.rs`). The house rule, stated in `lib.rs`'s own doc comment, is that every module except `compile.rs` is pure: `&str` in, typed data out, no filesystem or network access. That makes every parser trivially unit-testable — you hand it a string, you check the struct it returns. Each raw-data module (`kjv.rs`, `geo.rs`, `theographic.rs`, `xrefs.rs`, `people.rs`, `easton.rs`, `people_groups.rs`, `brainfuel.rs`, `concord.rs`, `kretzmann.rs`, `red_letter.rs`) targets one named external dataset. `curated.rs` parses this project's OWN hand-typed TOML files (eras, events, place histories, the catechism...). `validate.rs` is the fail-loud gate: it walks the fully-merged data and collects every problem (`Vec<String>`, an accumulator) rather than stopping at the first, so a curator fixing data sees the whole list at once. `compile.rs` is the one function that's allowed to touch disk — it orchestrates every parser and validator in order and hands back one `AtlasData` struct plus a coverage `Report`.
overview.l3: Workspace member depending on `atlas-core` (the shared type/canon crate) plus `serde`/`serde_json`/`toml`/`serde_yaml`/`anyhow`. `pub fn compile(raw_dir, curated_dir) -> Result<CompileOutput>` (compile.rs:71) is the single orchestration entry point three different callers use: `main.rs` (writes data/compiled/*.json + report.txt), `atlas-graph`'s `bins/compile_graph.rs`, and `atlas-server`'s `--build-from-raw` dev fallback — one code path, never three independently-drifting copies (compile.rs:1-31). M-C2 deleted five of the previously-written compiled JSON files (places/events/narratives/verses-kjv/cross-refs.json); that data now lives only on the compiled graph (`atlas-graph`), not in this crate's own output — `AtlasData` still carries it in memory for `validate::run` and the graph adapters. Determinism matters throughout: `xrefs::parse` sorts cross-refs by votes descending, `people::parse_people`/`people_groups::parse_people_groups` explicitly sort resolved verse links into canon order rather than trusting source-file order, and `polities::assign_color_keys` computes a collision-free palette assignment from the full sorted roster in one pass. Known scale/gap disclosures ride throughout the doc comments rather than being silently smoothed over (e.g. kretzmann.rs's over-excision guard, brainfuel.rs's KJV cross-check mismatch counts) — this codebase's 'scale honesty' convention. `tests/etl.rs` (2,280 lines) is the crate's main unit-level integration suite; `tests/coverage.rs`, `tests/*_real_data.rs`, and `tests/sources_validate.rs` run parsers against the REAL committed data files, not just synthetic fixtures.

files.l1: This is the crate's table of contents. files.role: the primary binary: calls compile(), writes data/compiled/*.json + report.txt
files.l1: This is the button you press to rebuild the atlas's data. Run it, and it reads every raw download plus every hand-typed curated file, checks everything for mistakes, and writes out the tidied files the rest of the app reads — plus a plain-text report showing how much data made it through and any problems found. This is the L1 story for 'how does the KJV text get in': this program calls compile(), which calls kjv::parse on the raw kjv.json file, and the resulting verse text ends up on the compiled AtlasData that eventually becomes the graph the reader/map serve from.
files.l2: `fn main() -> Result<()>` builds three `PathBuf`s (raw/curated/compiled directories, joined from parts rather than a literal string so path separators stay consistent on Windows), calls `compile::compile(&raw_dir, &curated_dir)`, then writes each surviving field of the returned `AtlasData` to its own JSON file via a small `write_json` helper (`serde_json::to_string_pretty` + `fs::write`). The `?` operator propagates any error from `compile()` straight out of `main`, so a validation failure anywhere in the pipeline aborts the whole build with a printed error chain (`anyhow::Context` adds a human-readable trail). Five files this binary used to write (places/events/narratives/verses-kjv/cross-refs.json) were deleted at 'M-C2' — that data now lives only on the compiled graph, not as a standalone JSON file; the doc comment explains this deletion explicitly.
files.l3: Uses `anyhow::{Context, Result}` for error propagation with `.with_context(|| ...)` closures that lazily format path-specific error messages. `write_json<T: serde::Serialize>(path, value)` (main.rs:72) is a small generic helper — `T: Serialize` is a trait bound restricting the function to types that know how to become JSON. Writes: canon.json, books-meta.json, chronology-anchors.json, book-narration-windows.json, polities.json, landmarks.json, place-history.json, place-names-kjv.json, land-mask.json, catechism.json, report.txt (also echoed to stdout via `print!`). `compile()`'s three extra return fields (`place_history_list`, `place_name_alias_list` alongside `data`/`report`) exist specifically so this file's own JSON writes stay in curated-file order rather than a HashMap's incidental iteration order.

files.role: shared helper: parses Book.Chapter.Verse OSIS-style references
files.l1: Different downloaded datasets refer to Bible verses using slightly different book-name spellings (one might call a book '2Kgs', matching an older international standard called OSIS, rather than this project's own '2KI'). This tiny file is the one place that turns any of those OSIS-style references into this project's own consistent verse identifier, so every other parser in the crate can rely on one shared, tested translator instead of reinventing it.
files.l2: Two public functions: `parse_verse(s: &str) -> Option<VerseId>` splits a string like `"2Kgs.5.12"` on `.`, resolves the book name via `atlas_core::canon::resolve_alias` (which matches by code OR OSIS abbreviation OR full name), and parses the chapter/verse numbers — returning `None` (Rust's 'maybe a value' type, used here instead of an error) on anything that doesn't fit the exact three-part shape, since callers decide for themselves whether a non-match is fatal or just a droppable row. `canonical(v: &VerseId) -> String` formats a `VerseId` back into this project's own canonical string form, e.g. `"2KI.5.12"`.
files.l3: `parse_verse` (osis.rs:21) uses `?`-chaining through `Option` (via `.split('.').collect()`, `resolve_alias(...)?`, `.parse().ok()?`) to short-circuit on any malformed piece. Rejects chapter/verse `0` explicitly (OSIS never uses 1-based-from-zero). Used by essentially every corpus adapter in the crate (`xrefs.rs`, `geo.rs`, `theographic.rs`, `people.rs`, `people_groups.rs`) as the one shared translator between an external dataset's OSIS spelling and `atlas_core::refs::VerseId`. Unit-tested for both the happy path (2Kgs.5.12 -> 2KI.5.12) and four distinct rejection shapes (wrong segment count, unknown book, chapter 0, verse 0).

files.role: parses the raw KJV JSON into the compiled Canon + verse-text map
files.l1: This is where the actual King James Bible text enters the app. The raw file (data/raw/kjv.json) is one big JSON object listing every book, chapter, and verse; this file reads it and produces two things: a canon table (book names, codes, and how many verses each chapter has) and a lookup from 'GEN.1.1' to the actual verse text. Every verse card the reader ever sees traces back to this one parse. Its book names ('I Samuel', 'Revelation of John') use an old-fashioned style, so this file also normalizes them before matching against the project's own book list.
files.l2: `parse(input: &str) -> Result<(Canon, HashMap<String, String>)>` deserializes the JSON via `serde`-derived `Deserialize` structs (`RawKjv`/`RawBook`/`RawChapter`/`RawVerse`), then for each book calls `normalize_book_name` to fix Roman-numeral prefixes ('I'/'II'/'III' -> '1'/'2'/'3') and strip an ' of John' suffix, then `atlas_core::canon::resolve_alias` to get a `BookId`. It builds a `HashMap<String, String>` keyed `"CODE.CHAPTER.VERSE"` and a `Canon` struct listing every book's chapter/verse counts, sorted into canonical book order regardless of the input file's own ordering (`books.sort_by_key`). A `bail!` (from `anyhow`) hard-errors if any book name can't be resolved even after normalization — there is no silent drop path for the base KJV text.
files.l3: `normalize_book_name` (kjv.rs:54) is `pub(crate)` (visible crate-wide but not outside it) specifically because `brainfuel.rs`'s `book_code_map` reuses it verbatim for `data/books.json`'s identically-styled `kjv_name` field — 'one normalizer, not two independently-authored copies that could drift' (doc comment). `parse` (kjv.rs:72) returns a tuple `(Canon, HashMap<String, String>)` rather than a combined struct since the two are consumed differently downstream (Canon feeds canon.json; the verse map feeds everything else and is never itself written to disk). Hard-fails via `bail!` on any unresolvable book name, unlike most other parsers in this crate that soft-drop unresolvable raw-data rows — the base KJV text is treated as too load-bearing to tolerate a silent drop.

files.role: parses openbible.info's cross-reference TSV into per-verse CrossRef lists
files.l1: This turns a giant spreadsheet of 'verse A points to verse B, with N votes' into the data behind the app's cross-reference feature — the little list of related verses you see when reading. It handles the tricky bits of the source file (some entries point to a range of verses, not just one; some rows are junk) and it makes sure results are sorted so the most agreed-upon cross-references show up first.
files.l2: `parse(input) -> Result<(HashMap<String, Vec<CrossRef>>, XrefStats)>` reads a tab-separated file, skipping its header row unconditionally (since real data rows have 3 tab fields but the header has 4). For each row it parses the 'From' verse and 'To' target (a single verse or a same-chapter/cross-chapter range, canonicalized by `parse_to_span`), drops the row if it's malformed or a self-reference, and sorts each verse's own cross-ref list by votes descending. `filter_missing_first_verse` is a second pure pass (no I/O) that drops any cross-ref whose target's first verse doesn't exist in the compiled KJV text — split out as its own function specifically so it stays unit-testable without needing the whole compiled verse map wired through `parse` itself.
files.l3: `XrefStats` (xrefs.rs:27) tracks `dropped_unparseable`/`dropped_self` — every drop is counted, never silent. `parse_to_span` (xrefs.rs:40) tries the whole `To` field as one verse first, then falls back to splitting on the first `-` for a range, producing three possible canonical forms: single verse, same-chapter range (`COL.1.16-17`), or cross-book range (`MAT.5.3-MAT.6.2`). `first_verse_of_target` (xrefs.rs:106) extracts just the first verse of an already-canonicalized target string, used by `filter_missing_first_verse` — this is a SECOND pure pass over the already-parsed map, run by `main.rs`/`compile.rs` after the KJV verse map is available, since `xrefs::parse` itself has no access to it (pure `&str`-in design).

files.role: parses OpenBible.info's ancient.jsonl geocoding bundle into compiled Places
files.l1: This turns a giant list of ancient-place-name guesses (each with possible modern-day coordinates and a confidence score) into the actual dots on the app's map. Many ancient places have several candidate modern locations; this file picks the best-scored one for each place. A place with no usable coordinate at all is simply left off the map rather than causing an error — geocoding coverage is naturally incomplete.
files.l2: `parse(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<Place>>` reads the file as JSON Lines (one JSON object per line, not a big array) and for each place calls `best_lonlat` to pick the highest-scoring `(lon, lat)` pair across all of that place's candidate 'identifications.' It builds a URL-friendly `id` via `kebab(name)` (lowercasing and hyphenating), handling name collisions by appending `-2`, `-3`, etc. It also filters each place's KJV verse links down to only verses whose translations list includes `"kjv"`, deduping as it goes via `osis::parse_verse`/`osis::canonical`.
files.l3: `RawAncient`/`RawIdentification`/`RawResolution`/`RawModernAssoc`/`RawVerseLink` (geo.rs:25-64) are the `#[derive(Deserialize)]` structs mirroring the real JSON shape, with several `Option`/`#[serde(default)]` fields to handle a `"special": "not_a_place"` dead-end resolution that carries neither `lonlat` nor `modern_basis_id` at all. `best_lonlat` (geo.rs:91) walks every `identifications[].resolutions[]`, scoring each by `modern_associations[modern_basis_id].score` (default 0 if unknown), keeping the first-encountered on a tie. The module doc comment discloses a divergence from `data/raw/README.md`'s own worked example: the README describes `identifications[].score` as a plain int, but the real file nests it as a stats object, and the actually-used per-modern-id score lives at `modern_associations{modern_id}.score` instead — a real finding from data scouting, corrected in the README too.

files.role: parses/validates data/curated/sources.toml against LICENSES.md
files.l1: The app's Sources page needs one authoritative list of where every dataset came from and what license it's under. This file reads that curated list and cross-checks it word-for-word against LICENSES.md's own table, so the two documents can never silently drift apart — if someone adds a source to one file but forgets the other, the build fails loudly instead of shipping a page that quietly disagrees with the license file.
files.l2: Three public functions: `parse_sources` (TOML -> `SourcesDocument`, a plain structural parse), `validate_structure` (checks for duplicate ids, an undeclared category reference, an empty licenses_row_key, and — for the provenance join table — an undeclared source or off-vocabulary confidence value), and `validate_against_licenses` (the real cross-file check: extracts every data row of LICENSES.md's own '## Per-source table' and requires an exact 1:1 match against `sources.toml` entries by `licenses_row_key`, a literal substring match). Kept as its own module, deliberately never wired into the main `compile()` pipeline, since this data has nothing to do with the Bible graph itself.
files.l3: `extract_per_source_table_rows` (sources.rs:112) is a small Markdown-table scraper: finds the `## Per-source table` heading, slices to the next `## ` heading, and reads every `|`-prefixed line as a row, skipping the header and separator rows by position (first two data-looking rows). `validate_against_licenses` (sources.rs:151) builds a `matched_row_for_source: Vec<Option<usize>>` and walks every LICENSES.md row, requiring `licenses_row_key` to match EXACTLY ONE source (an ambiguous or zero-match row both `bail!`), then separately checks every source got matched. Runs from two places that must never drift: `gen_sources`'s binary (regenerating sources.json) and `tests/sources_validate.rs` (so `cargo test --workspace` alone catches drift with nothing extra to remember to run).

files.role: joins Theographic's events/places/verses tables into compiled Events
files.l1: This is where dated events (the Exodus, the Fall of Jerusalem, and hundreds more) enter the app, sourced from a free Bible database called Theographic. That database uses its own internal reference numbers to link an event to its place and its verses, so this file's main job is following those links, converting the dates into this project's own year format, and — when an event's place isn't already one of the map's dots — creating a brand-new place for it on the spot.
files.l2: `parse_events(places_json, verses_json, events_json, place_slug_by_name) -> Result<(Vec<Event>, Vec<Place>, TheoStats)>` deserializes three separate JSON files (an Airtable-style export, so every record is `{id, fields}`), then for each event resolves its place-name references (case-insensitive match against the caller's own compiled place list) and its verse references (through the verses table's own `osisRef`, via `osis::parse_verse`). An event place with no name match gets a brand-new `Place` synthesized straight from Theographic's own lat/lon (note: normal lat,lon order here, unlike OpenBible's lon,lat convention). Dates use an 'astronomical year' convention (`-4003` means `4004 BC`) which `parse_theo_year` converts to this project's own historical (no-year-zero) numbering.
files.l3: `parse_theo_year` (theographic.rs:96) is `pub(crate)` specifically because `people::parse_people` reuses it verbatim for birth/death years — the SAME Theographic astronomical-year convention, so a second independently-authored copy would only risk drift, never add real independence. Handles three input shapes: bare astronomical integer (`"-4003"`), a literal `"NNNN BC"` calendar year (no shift), and an ISO-ish `"0030-05-01"` form (extracts the leading year). `TheoStats` (theographic.rs:73) tracks total/dated/undated/no_place/new_places — every drop or synthesis is counted, never silent. files.l1: This brings in Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897, public domain) — the short encyclopedia-style descriptions you might see for a person or place elsewhere in the app. Each dictionary entry is tagged as matching a specific person, a specific place, several possible things at once ('multi'), or nothing recognizable ('unmatched'); this file resolves the person/place tags to this project's own ids where it safely can, and never guesses when a match is genuinely ambiguous.

files.role: geometry helpers for curated polity borders: color assignment + ring simplicity checking
files.l1: This is the toolkit behind the map's colored kingdom borders. Each hand-drawn kingdom (Egypt, Assyria, Babylon...) needs a border shape that doesn't cross itself, and a distinct color so no two overlapping kingdoms look the same. This file provides both: a check that a hand-typed list of coordinates forms a sensible, non-self-crossing shape, and an algorithm that assigns every kingdom a color guaranteed different from every other kingdom's, every single build.
files.l2: Two main pieces. `assign_color_keys(sorted_ids: &[&str]) -> Vec<u8>` computes a deterministic starting color 'bucket' for each polity id (`color_seed`, a hash summing Unicode code points, mod 16 palette slots) then linear-probes forward from that seed to find the first free bucket no earlier id in the same call already claimed — guaranteeing every polity gets a distinct color as long as there are 16 or fewer polities. `ring_is_simple(ring: &[(f64, f64)]) -> bool` implements the standard CCW/orientation-based segment-intersection test (a classic algorithm from Cormen et al.) to detect whether a hand-drawn border ring crosses itself (a 'bowtie' shape) — reused from an earlier one-off Node.js script, now a permanent, automatic build-time check instead of something a curator has to remember to run by hand.
files.l3: `BIBLICAL_WORLD_BBOX` (polities.rs:48) is a `pub const Bbox` carried over byte-for-byte from a retired module and cross-referenced with `client/wwwroot/js/map.js`'s own `BIBLICAL_WORLD_BOUNDS` constant — the two MUST be kept in sync if the compiled place extent ever changes. `assign_color_keys` (polities.rs:141) requires `sorted_ids` already sorted by the caller (main.rs's own filename/id order) for determinism — 'same data, same colors, every run,' verified by tests over the real 14-polity roster plus synthetic rosters up to and past the 16-slot palette size (graceful degradation to a collision, never a panic, once id count exceeds 16). `ring_is_simple` (polities.rs:227) is O(n²) over ring edges, entirely adequate at this app's 30-90-point-per-ring scale; handles both closed (first point repeated) and open ring representations.

files.role: parses the vendored KJV OSIS XML into per-verse red-letter (words of Jesus) spans
files.l1: This adds the 'red letter' feature: marking exactly which words in the KJV text are Jesus speaking, verse by verse, sometimes down to which part of a verse. It reads a specially-marked public-domain KJV file and, for every span the source marks as Jesus's own words, finds the matching text in this project's own official KJV verse text — never trusting the source's own copy of the words, only using it to find WHERE in our text the red starts and stops.
files.l2: `parse(xml, kjv_verses: &HashMap<String,String>) -> Result<RedLetterCorpus>` is a hand-rolled XML tag scanner (this crate never uses an XML parsing library) that tracks the current book/chapter/verse as it walks the file and, for each verse, records raw `<q who="Jesus">` span texts. The moment a verse closes, `align_verse` searches for each span's own trimmed text as a substring of OUR canonical verse text, first case-sensitively then (if that fails) case-insensitively — resolving to a byte-offset range into OUR bytes, never storing a byte of the source's own copy. A span that matches neither way is dropped from the output but the verse itself STAYS in the verse set (the verse-content 'has red words' fact is independent of alignment success).
files.l3: `attr`/`has_attr` (red_letter.rs:138/150) have a documented self-caught bug guard: searching for `" sID=\""` (leading space) rather than bare `"sID=\""`, since `sID=` is a literal trailing substring of `osisID=` and a naive search would silently match inside the WRONG attribute. `align_verse` (red_letter.rs:236) advances a cursor across successful matches so two spans in one verse (narration between two sayings) resolve left-to-right rather than both collapsing onto the first occurrence. `ascii_ci_find`/`ascii_ci_eq` deliberately avoid `str::to_lowercase()` since it's Unicode-aware and can change a string's own BYTE LENGTH, which would break offset math — only ASCII letters are treated case-insensitively. `contiguous_ranges` (red_letter.rs:422) groups the verse set into maximal contiguous canon-order ranges for a SpokenBy row shape, correctly detecting a chapter rollover via a caller-supplied `chapter_verse_counts` closure rather than assuming exactly verse+1. The module doc comment discloses 18 of 2,081 real spans (0.87%) that fail both alignment tiers — every one a real spelling/punctuation variant (Caesar/Cesar, Judaea/Judea, one source-side typo), never a content substitution.

files.role: parses parallel Bible editions (Vulgate, Masoretic, Douay-Rheims, Finnish, Swedish, Textus Receptus) + the KJV case-restoration pass
files.l1: This brings in five other historic Bible translations, aligned verse-for-verse against our own KJV, from a vendored open dataset that already lines them all up. It also does something specific and careful: it reads that same dataset's OWN copy of the KJV text purely to compare against our official KJV — never to change a WORD of it, only to restore the correct capitalization pattern (like 'LORD' in all-caps where the KJV convention calls for it) when this app's own imported text lost that capitalization along the way. The project's own rule (the 'KJV inerrancy directive') is: never touch the actual words, only ever fix the letter case, and only when it's provably safe to do so.
files.l2: `read_all(root) -> Result<BrainFuelCorpus>` walks every `bible/{ot,nt}/{CODE}/{NNN}.json` chapter file (929 OT + 260 NT, pre-aligned to KJV verse positions) and for each verse records which of six editions has real text at that position, tracking three states per edition: present (a real rendering), absent (a documented per-verse gap, e.g. verses merged in the Vulgate tradition), or not-applicable (the edition doesn't apply to that testament at all). `restore_verse_case(ours, theirs) -> Option<String>` is the core case-restoration primitive: returns `None` unless the two texts are equal ignoring ASCII case, then transfers `theirs`'s exact case pattern onto `ours`'s own bytes one-for-one. `classify_and_restore` extends this to a second class — a folded-in Psalm superscription our text keeps but the comparison source doesn't — via `tail_align`, restoring only the aligned tail, never the superscription itself.
files.l3: `RenderingOutcome`/`VerseRow.field()` (brainfuel.rs:213/229) route each of six possible edition fields through one shared classification. `restore_verse_case` (brainfuel.rs:485) is provably UTF-8-safe: `eq_ignore_ascii_case` requires equal byte length so the zipped byte streams stay aligned, and every byte it CHANGES is guaranteed single-byte ASCII on both sides, so a non-ASCII continuation byte is never touched. `SUPERSCRIPTION_EXCLUSIONS` (brainfuel.rs:539) is a small, disclosed, hand-authored exclusion table — three positions that WOULD tail-align but are known brain-fuel transcription artifacts (an all-caps rendering quirk, a real versification-boundary coincidence at ACT.9.29), checked BEFORE `tail_align` runs. `king_james_by_dot_ref` exposes the raw comparison column for `atlas_graph::fidelity`'s own independent re-derivation, so the SAME transform (never a second copy) backs both the ETL restoration pass and the graph's own fidelity check.

files.role: the one orchestration function: reads raw+curated, merges, hard-validates, returns AtlasData
files.l1: This is the assembly line. It calls every single parser in this crate in the right order, joins their outputs together (attaching events to their places, merging cross-references, folding in curated hand-typed corrections), runs every validation check, and hands back one complete, checked bundle of data. Three different programs call this exact same function rather than each having their own copy — so there's only one true build process, never several that could quietly disagree.
files.l2: `pub fn compile(raw_dir, curated_dir) -> Result<CompileOutput>` runs, in order: (1) every raw-data parser (kjv, geo, theographic, people, easton, people_groups, xrefs), (2) every curated-TOML parser (eras, chronology anchors, book windows, books, events-extra, narratives, people-group seeds, fulfillments, typology), (3) a long merge phase joining events to witnesses, applying an 'account vs. mention' retype correction, merging Acts/Atlas section provenance, then (4) `atlas_core::merge`/`event_merge`/`nt_calibration`/`chronology` corrections applied to the merged data, (5) `AtlasData::new(...).finish()` plus `validate::run`, and finally (6) polities/landmarks/land-mask/place-history/place-names-kjv/catechism, each with its own dedicated `validate::run_*` call. Every step's error is wrapped with `.context(...)` naming exactly which curated file to fix.
files.l3: `process_polities` (compile.rs:575) reads every `data/curated/polities/*.toml` file in sorted filename order (deterministic report order), computes `PolityStats`, then calls `polities::assign_color_keys` over the FULL sorted id roster in one pass (color assignment needs global visibility, so it's deliberately not done per-file in `curated::parse_polity`). `check_curated_inputs_exist` (compile.rs:656) is a defensive pre-flight check listing every required curated file/directory by name, so a missing file fails with one clear list rather than a confusing downstream parse error. The 'ATTEST-1' account-vs-mention retype (compile.rs:190-249) is the pipeline's most delicate step: it strips named verses from an event's `verses` AND every witness row's translations in the SAME pass, since a stale correction that only strips one side would silently leave the other alive — with a disclosed known limitation that the match is exact-string, so a verse living INSIDE a stored range entry (`LUK.1.26-38`) won't be caught by the retype.

files.role: parsers for every data/curated/*.toml schema this project hand-authors
files.l1: This is where every piece of this project's OWN hand-typed content gets read in — its list of historical eras, its own extra events not covered by the downloaded database, place histories (when a city changed names), the borders of kingdoms, the catechism text itself, and more. Each of these has its own small TOML file format, and this file has one function per format. Because this is the project's own authored data, mistakes are held to a strict bar: a badly-shaped file fails the build immediately rather than being quietly skipped.
files.l2: One `pub fn parse_*` function per curated schema (about 20 of them): `parse_eras`, `parse_chronology_anchors`, `parse_book_narration_windows`, `parse_books`, `parse_narrative`, `parse_events_extra`, `parse_event_witnesses`, `parse_attestation_corrections`, `parse_acts_sections`, `parse_atlas_sections`, `parse_coverage_manifest`, `parse_landmarks`, `parse_place_history`, `parse_place_names_kjv`, `parse_polity`, `parse_land_mask`, `parse_catechism`, `parse_catechism_mapping`, `parse_catechism_deut5`, `parse_people_group_seeds`, `parse_fulfillments`, `parse_typology`. Most deserialize straight into `atlas_core::data` structs whose field names already match the TOML schema. A shared helper, `expand_verse_ref`, turns a curator-friendly single-verse-or-range string (`"EXO.14.21-31"`) into individual canonical verse ids, reused across several of these schemas rather than reimplemented per-file.
files.l3: Every parser here follows a consistent split: parse structurally here (bail loud on malformed TOML), defer any cross-reference check needing the fuller compiled picture (a real place id, a real event id, the compiled KJV text) to `validate::run_*` — this is stated explicitly in nearly every function's own doc comment. `parse_events_extra` (curated.rs:247) has a Batch T2 conditional-required rule: `kind = "general"` FORBIDS `from_year`/`to_year`/`places` (a dateless/placeless titled container must not fabricate a date), while `kind = "event"` (default) REQUIRES all three — enforced structurally in both directions, not by convention. `parse_polity` (curated.rs:810) deliberately leaves `color_key` at a provisional `0`; only `process_polities` (compile.rs) assigns the real, collision-free value once every polity in the roster is visible at once. `parse_place_names_kjv`/`parse_event_witnesses`/`parse_acts_sections` are all deliberately FLAT arrays with an explicit id per row (never nested under a parent array-of-tables) — the doc comment explains this dodges a real TOML footgun (`[era.transition]`/`[era.fall]` attaching to whichever `[[era]]` was MOST RECENTLY OPENED, which shipped a real bug once, 7 of 22 deltas).

files.role: hard validation of the fully-merged AtlasData before it's written to disk
files.l1: This is the project's quality gate. After everything has been read and joined together, this file checks the WHOLE result for mistakes: an event pointing at a place that doesn't exist, two overlapping time periods, a duplicate id, a typo'd Bible verse reference, two 'different' events that are secretly duplicates of each other. It never stops at the first problem it finds — it collects every single one and reports them all together, so a curator fixing the data sees the whole list in one build instead of playing whack-a-mole one error at a time.
files.l2: `pub fn run(data: &AtlasData) -> Result<()>` is the main check, covering duplicate place/event ids, events referencing unknown places, non-canonical verse ids, era gaps/overlaps/coverage of the full year span, dangling narrative legs, and non-chronological narrative ordering. A dozen more `pub fn run_*` functions each validate one separate curated schema that needs its own extra context the main `run` doesn't have (the clip bounding box, the compiled KJV text, the full compiled place list): `run_landmarks`, `run_polities`, `run_land_mask`, `run_place_history`, `run_place_names_kjv`, `run_catechism`, `run_place_merges`, `run_event_merges`, `run_cross_book_duplicates`, `run_no_two_opinions`, `run_chronology_anchors`, `run_chronology_anchor_equality`, `run_chronology_windows`, `run_era_boundaries`. Every function follows the SAME shape: build a `Vec<String>` of errors, keep going instead of returning early, then `bail!` once at the end listing every violation found.
files.l3: `check_duplicate_ids`/`check_eras` (validate.rs:1345/1358) are small shared helpers used by several `run_*` functions. `run_event_merges` (validate.rs:947) and `run_cross_book_duplicates` (validate.rs:1079) are two INDEPENDENT duplicate-event detectors — the doc comment explains why a second detector is needed: `verse_jaccard` is structurally blind to a same-occurrence pair citing disjoint verse sets (different books, or a small subset fully contained in a larger sibling), which `cross_book_duplicate_candidate`'s title-similarity check catches instead. `run_no_two_opinions` (validate.rs:1147) is 'THE CHRONOLOGY AUTHORITY LAW's own DIRECT enforcement — it runs on the FINAL, post-merge, post-calibration event set a reader actually sees (not the pre-merge set the other two duplicate-detectors need), asserting no two surviving events with heavy witness overlap carry disagreeing placements unless explicitly documented as genuinely distinct. `run_place_names_kjv` (validate.rs:694) enforces a 'verbatim-substring law': every curated KJV alias string must be a case-sensitive verbatim substring of the actual KJV text of every verse listed for it, with en/em dash normalization disclosed as necessary for one real pre-existing curated row.

files.role: parses Kretzmann's Popular Commentary (1,189 pages, two HTML templates) into verse-anchored commentary units
files.l1: This brings in an entire public-domain Bible commentary — a paragraph or more of explanation for nearly every passage, written by Paul Kretzmann in the early 1900s — and ties each piece of commentary to the exact verse or verses it discusses. The source website renders the Old and New Testaments slightly differently (one quotes short Bible phrases mid-sentence, the other quotes whole verses in a block first), so this file has to understand and reconcile both styles. It also runs an important safety check afterward: it reassembles what it excised as 'quoted Bible text' and compares it back against the official KJV text, to prove that no Bible content was silently altered while stripping the quotes out.
files.l2: `parse_chapter(html, book_index, chapter, chapter_verse_count, kjv_verses) -> Result<ParsedChapter>` is the central function: a single document-order walk over recognized 'segments' (heading, a bold KJV-quote span, a blockquote-style KJV-quote paragraph, or plain commentary text between them) that builds up `KretzUnit`s (id, verse range, heading, and Kretzmann's own prose ONLY — never a byte of quoted KJV text) plus separately-tracked `ExcisedFragment`s (the removed quotes, kept only for the fidelity check). `check_conservation(fragments, canonical) -> ConservationReport` reassembles each verse's fragments and compares them against the real canonical verse text through three tiers: exact match, then case+punctuation-normalized match, then a curated table of American/British spelling variants (`SPELLING_VARIANTS`) — anything failing all three is a disclosed `Mismatch`, never silently ignored.
files.l3: `OVER-EXCISION GUARD` (`apply_over_excision_guard`, kretzmann.rs:1550): a real self-caught bug class — the digital edition occasionally bolds Kretzmann's OWN short connective gloss alongside the quoted clause, which a naive quote-excision would silently destroy as if it were KJV text; this recovers the non-matching tail back into stored prose instead, using a word-tokenized longest-common-block alignment (`longest_common_block`/`align_recursive`, kretzmann.rs:1487-1549) against the real canonical verse. `find_inline_verse_marker` (kretzmann.rs:586) is a second, later fix (fix round 2): the source occasionally renders a mid-sentence verse boundary as literal text ('v. 61') instead of a proper tag, which used to silently swallow the whole following verse into the preceding fragment — recognized only when the cited number is EXACTLY the next verse after the currently-open one, so an ordinary backward cross-reference ('v. 7' inside a later verse's own lemma) is never mistaken for a boundary. `compose_reading_view`/`strip_comment_blocks` (kretzmann.rs:1700/1727) implement a second, independent law (KRETZ-ACCEPT-2): composing verse-plus-comment segments and then stripping every comment must reproduce the canonical Bible text exactly, proving the reading-view construction itself (not just the parse) never mutates verse text. `extract_date_clauses` (kretzmann.rs:1771) mines B.C./A.D./Anno Mundi dating clauses out of stored prose, parsing-only, never interpreting a reign-year formula into a numeric year.

files.l1: This runs the parallel-Bible-editions parser against the actual downloaded files (not fake test data) and locks in the exact numbers found: how many verses per edition, how many marked gaps, and — most importantly — exactly how many places brain-fuel's own copy of the KJV text disagrees with our official KJV text, both before and after the careful letter-case-only correction pass.
files.l2: Builds the real corpus once (`corpus()`, a cached helper) and real KJV verse map (`our_kjv_verses()`), then asserts exact pinned counts: total chapter files, total verse rows, per-edition present/absent counts, zero anomalies, and the KJV cross-check mismatch counts before and after case restoration. Several tests spot-check specific verses byte-for-byte against the real source HTML.
files.l3: `case_restoration_satisfies_the_case_only_law_over_every_real_position` is a property test over the WHOLE real corpus (not a spot check) proving the KJV inerrancy directive holds everywhere the restoration pass touches: before/after must be identical under ASCII case-folding at every touched position. `superscription_exclusions_are_provably_untouched` proves the three hand-authored exclusion-table entries genuinely restore nothing. `real_absent_marker_example_1_chronicles_11_47` pins one specific documented real gap.

files.role: real-data tests over the full 1,189-page Kretzmann commentary corpus
files.l1: This runs the commentary parser against every one of the 1,189 real downloaded pages and pins the exact resulting numbers, including the crucial fidelity check: comparing every excised quoted-Bible-text fragment back against the real KJV to prove Kretzmann's commentary content never silently swallowed or altered actual Scripture. It also spot-checks a few famous or tricky verses individually.
files.l2: Builds the real corpus (`real_corpus`), the real KJV verse map (`real_kjv_verses`), and the real restored canonical text (`real_canonical`) once via cached helpers, then asserts pinned totals for units/fragments/footnotes/over-excisions/inline-verse-markers, runs `check_conservation` over the whole real corpus and pins its exact exact/mechanical/mechanical_spelling/mismatch counts, and spot-checks specific verses (Genesis 1:2's three-way split, Psalm 110:1's Tetragrammaton case restoration, John 3:16 as a Type-B block quote example).
files.l3: `kretz_accept_1_conservation_law_over_the_whole_real_corpus_has_the_pinned_shape` is the load-bearing fidelity assertion — the exact/mechanical/mechanical_spelling/mismatch counts (2,525/23,606/1,903/2,998 as of the last fix round, per the file's own doc comment) are pinned as a REGRESSION HARNESS that 'moves only with a disclosed reason,' never asserted as zero mismatches (which the doc comment calls dishonest at this data scale). `over_excision_guard_recovers_exo_20_12_and_rut_4_11_prose_verbatim_against_the_source_html` and `mat_26_60_to_61_inline_verse_marker_lands_as_v61_lemma_not_v60_prose_end_to_end` are end-to-end regression tests for the two documented self-caught bug fixes (fix rounds 1 and 2). `kretz_accept_2_composed_reading_view_strips_to_exactly_the_whole_canonical_bible` proves the second, independent law over the whole real corpus.
